items.readable_text:
Content:
We know how to define the double integral of a function over a rectangular domain. Now, we'll learn how to define a double integral over a non-rectangular region.

Content:
Let's consider the non-rectangular region [MATH: D] enclosed by the circle [MATH: x^2+y^2=1] in the first quadrant, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/da4c46a5901ac362a413078cffa326fd]

Content:
We will define the following double integral over this non-rectangular region:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{D} (3-x^2-y^2) \, \textrm{d}A]

Content:
To do this, we will use the following trick. Let's enclose the region [MATH: D] by a rectangle [MATH: R] with sides parallel to the coordinates axes, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6dfc82221f7753e2325902813d7f04da]

Content:
Now, we extend our function to [MATH: R] by setting a new function [MATH: f(x,y)] that's equal to [MATH: 0] outside [MATH: D] and equals [MATH: 3-x^2-y^2] on [MATH: D\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: {3 − x^{2} − y^{2},|(x, y) ∈ R∩D; 0,|(x, y) ∈ R∖D]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/afafca53a3a338cae729d628fea0b1db]

Content:
Although [MATH: f(x,y)] might not be continuous at the boundary of [MATH: D,] the double integral of [MATH: f(x,y)] over the rectangular domain [MATH: R] will exist.

Content:
Therefore, we define our double integral of [MATH: 3-x^2-y^2] over [MATH: D] as

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_D (3-x^2-y^2) \, \textrm{d}A = \iint\limits_R f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A.]

Content:
Geometrically, the value of the double integral will give us the volume of the solid bounded by the surface [MATH: z=3-x^2-y^2] over the quarter-circular domain [MATH: D.]

Content:
Watch out! The domain [MATH: R] must not necessarily be the smallest possible rectangle that covers the region [MATH: D.] It can be any rectangular domain that covers [MATH: D] completely.

items.title: Determining a Valid Region to Define a Double Integral Over a Non-Rectangular Domain

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the region [MATH: D] shown above. If [MATH: {x^{2} − y^{2},|(x, y) ∈ R∩D; 0,|(x, y) ∈ R∖D] which of the following could be the definition of the rectangular domain [MATH: R?]

  1. [MATH: R=[-2,2] \times [-2,1]]

  2. [MATH: R=[-2,1] \times [-2,2]]

  3. [MATH: R=[-1,1] \times [-1,1]]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/f62ea4c35fcc7d18eac85d6d253ef727]

Consider the region [MATH: D] shown above. If
[MATH: {x^{2} − y^{2},|(x, y) ∈ R∩D; 0,|(x, y) ∈ R∖D]
which of the following could be the definition of the rectangular domain [MATH: R?]

1. [MATH: R=[-2,2] \times [-2,1]]
2. [MATH: R=[-2,1] \times [-2,2]]
3. [MATH: R=[-1,1] \times [-1,1]]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that if [MATH: R] covers [MATH: D] completely and we define

[MATH: {x^{2} − y^{2},|(x, y) ∈ R∩D; 0,|(x, y) ∈ R∖D,]

then, we obtain

[MATH: \iint\limits_D (x^2-y^2) \: \text{d}A = \iint\limits_R f(x,y) \: \text{d}A.]

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given rectangles.

  • Rectangles I and II cover the region [MATH: D] completely.

  • Rectangle III does not cover the region [MATH: D.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

  1. [MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{\large R} \cos(x-y) \: \text{d}A = \iint\limits_{\large D} f(x,y) \: \text{d}A,\quad] where [MATH: R=[-4,4] \times [-4,4]]

  2. [MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{\large D} \cos(x-y) \: \text{d}A = \iint\limits_{\large R} f(x,y) \: \text{d}A,\quad] where [MATH: R=[-2,2] \times [-2,2]]

  3. [MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{\large D} \cos(x-y) \: \text{d}A = \iint\limits_{\large R} f(x,y) \: \text{d}A,\quad] where [MATH: R=[-3,3] \times [-3,3]]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We know how to define the double integral of a function over a rectangular domain. Now, we'll learn how to define a double integral over a non-rectangular region.

Content:
Let's consider the non-rectangular region [MATH: D] enclosed by the circle [MATH: x^2+y^2=1] in the first quadrant, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/da4c46a5901ac362a413078cffa326fd]

Content:
We will define the following double integral over this non-rectangular region:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{D} (3-x^2-y^2) \, \textrm{d}A]

Content:
To do this, we will use the following trick. Let's enclose the region [MATH: D] by a rectangle [MATH: R] with sides parallel to the coordinates axes, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6dfc82221f7753e2325902813d7f04da]

Content:
Now, we extend our function to [MATH: R] by setting a new function [MATH: f(x,y)] that's equal to [MATH: 0] outside [MATH: D] and equals [MATH: 3-x^2-y^2] on [MATH: D\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: {3 − x^{2} − y^{2},|(x, y) ∈ R∩D; 0,|(x, y) ∈ R∖D]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/afafca53a3a338cae729d628fea0b1db]

Content:
Although [MATH: f(x,y)] might not be continuous at the boundary of [MATH: D,] the double integral of [MATH: f(x,y)] over the rectangular domain [MATH: R] will exist.

Content:
Therefore, we define our double integral of [MATH: 3-x^2-y^2] over [MATH: D] as

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_D (3-x^2-y^2) \, \textrm{d}A = \iint\limits_R f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A.]

Content:
Geometrically, the value of the double integral will give us the volume of the solid bounded by the surface [MATH: z=3-x^2-y^2] over the quarter-circular domain [MATH: D.]

Content:
Watch out! The domain [MATH: R] must not necessarily be the smallest possible rectangle that covers the region [MATH: D.] It can be any rectangular domain that covers [MATH: D] completely.

---

[MATH: {x^{2} − y^{2},|(x, y) ∈ R∩D; 0,|(x, y) ∈ R∖D,]

then, we obtain

[MATH: \iint\limits_D (x^2-y^2) \: \text{d}A = \iint\limits_R f(x,y) \: \text{d}A.]

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given rectangles.
